Executive Foundation and Regulatory Architecture of Probability Sampling

Statistical sampling (SS) in United States federal research and development (R&D) tax credit administration is a mathematically rigorous estimation technique used to determine Qualified Research Expenditures (QREs) under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41 when examining an entire population of research projects, employees, or contractor costs is operationally impractical due to data volume. Formally governed by Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Revenue Procedure 2011-42 (Rev. Proc. 2011-42, 2011-37 I.R.B. 318), probability sampling allows taxpayers and examining agents to select a randomized subset of units from a defined population, perform an exhaustive technical and financial audit on those selected units, and mathematically extrapolate the resulting qualification ratio to the total population value.

The strategic necessity of probability sampling arises from the tension between the strict substantiation mandate of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d) (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d))—which cross-references the general record-retention mandate of IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1—and the decentralized nature of modern enterprise R&D data. For large enterprises executing thousands of concurrent engineering tasks or employing hundreds of technical personnel across multiple cost centers, a 100% population review imposes compliance costs that can rival or exceed the economic value of the tax credit itself. Rather than attempting to document every project or employee hour across an entire enterprise, statistical sampling enables a focused allocation of engineering and tax accounting resources toward the rigorous substantiation of a manageable, scientifically selected subset of costs. Under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.02(1), the appropriateness of using a probability sample is a facts-and-circumstances determination weighing the time required to analyze large volumes of data, the cost of analyzing that data, and whether other books or records independently exist that possess greater probative value. Probability samples are generally not appropriate where evidence is readily available from another source that provides a more accurate answer, or where the use of sampling does not conform to applicable financial accounting standards such as Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP).

At the initial tier of 500 R&D projects, a 100% review requires 1,000 review hours compared to 300 hours for a 150-unit statistical sample, saving 700 hours and yielding a 70.0% labor efficiency gain. At the intermediate tier of 2,500 projects, full-population review requires 5,000 hours versus 300 sample hours, saving 4,700 hours (a 94.0% efficiency gain). At the baseline scenario of 5,000 R&D projects, a 100% population audit requires 10,000 review hours compared to 300 hours for a 150-unit statistical sample, representing a 97.0% reduction in compliance labor and saving 9,700 engineering and tax review hours. Across the upper threshold of 10,000 projects, full-population substantiation demands 20,000 hours of review, whereas probability sampling maintains a 300-hour review burden, saving 19,700 hours and achieving a 98.5% labor efficiency gain.

When a taxpayer files an original return or refund claim grounded in a probability sample that adheres to Rev. Proc. 2011-42, the IRS examination process is substantially narrowed. Rather than issuing broad Information Document Requests (IDRs) spanning every engineering group, examination teams typically restrict their substantive audit inquiries to the specific units selected within the taxpayer's sample, which accelerates the IDR process and expedites audit closure. However, this procedural streamlining is governed by three strict legal and regulatory constraints that separate administrative audit efficiency from substantive tax law entitlement.

First, any statistical sample utilized by a taxpayer on an original return or refund claim is subject to mandatory validation by an IRS Computer Audit Specialist (CAS). As codified in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG): Credit for Increasing Research Activities and the Large Business and International (LB&I) Field Directive on the Use of Sampling Methodologies in Research Credit Cases, no taxpayer-prepared probability sample is accepted at face value; its mathematical design, randomization seed, stratification boundaries, and execution must be reviewed and confirmed for validity by the CAS. During agency-initiated sampling examinations, the CAS also collaborates directly with the IRS examination manager and the taxpayer to design a sampling plan that balances required statistical accuracy against a practical number of units to examine. Furthermore, Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.05(3) establishes that fatal errors in statistical methodology render a probability sample invalid, restricting the Service to considering unit findings strictly on an actual, non-extrapolated basis.

Second, probability sampling serves solely as an estimation tool for the quantum of qualified expenditures and never functions as a waiver of the substantive statutory requirements under IRC § 41(d). Every sampled unit must independently satisfy the four-part statutory test separately for each business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A): the Section 174 test requiring that expenditures represent research and experimental activities directed at eliminating uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design; the technological-in-nature test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B) requiring that the process of discovering information fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science; the qualified purpose test requiring that the research be intended to develop a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component; and the process-of-experimentation test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) requiring that substantially all of the activities constitute elements of an evaluative process of experimentation. In addition, the taxpayer must establish a verifiable nexus between the extrapolated qualified expenses—such as in-house research wages, supplies, computer rental or lease costs, or contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(1) and IRC § 41(b)(3)—and the underlying qualified research activities conducted at the business component level.

Third, Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.05(6), the IRS Research Credit ATG, and the Instructions for Form 6765 explicitly reiterate that deploying a statistical sample does not relieve the taxpayer of its foundational statutory obligation under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) to retain books, records, and documentation sufficient to substantiate expenditures across the entire population subject to the claim. While sampling narrows administrative examination in practice, IRS examiners retain the legal entitlement under the Research Credit ATG to request and receive records substantiating all expenses and activities to which the credit claim relates, even when those records fall outside the sampled subset itself.
Regulatory Foundations: Rev. Proc. 2011-42, Statistical Risk, and the Consent Divide
Probability Sampling Versus Judgment Sampling

Federal tax administration draws a sharp legal and mathematical boundary between statistical (probability) sampling and non-statistical (judgment) sampling. Under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.02(2)(b), statistical sampling relies on random probability selection in which every sampling unit in the population frame has a known, non-zero chance of selection using either simple random sampling or stratified random sampling, enabling objective quantification of sampling risk through confidence and precision metrics. Judgment sampling, conversely, selects units based on subjective reviewer criteria rather than probability theory, rendering sampling error mathematically unmeasurable.

Because a valid statistical sample under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 and Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) 42(18) guidelines provides an objective mathematical measure of estimation risk, the IRS, Chief Counsel, and the Department of Justice regard its extrapolated adjustments as legally sound and administratively defensible without requiring the taxpayer's written consent to apply the sample outcome. The LB&I Field Directive specifically recommends statistical sampling for research credit examinations involving more than 50 sampling units. In contrast, because a judgment sample relies on subjective selection criteria and lacks inherent statistical defensibility, an IRS examiner cannot project the results of a judgment sample to an underlying population unless the taxpayer provides explicit written consent—typically negotiated early in the examination with the assistance of local IRS counsel and executed via a formal closing agreement on IRS Form 906 (Closing Agreement on Final Determination Covering Specific Matters)—specifying both the methodology used and how its findings will be applied to the total population. While a judgment sample may appear less resource-intensive to execute initially, the requirement of mandatory taxpayer assent shifts the negotiation dynamic during audit resolution: if a taxpayer initially cooperates with a judgment sample but later objects without a signed Form 906 in place, adjustments projected from the judgment sample may not be sustainable in court, whereas a Rev. Proc. 2011-42 probability sample yields an independent administrative determination. Additionally, the IRS Research Credit ATG notes that the use of alternative sampling methodologies may be constrained if the taxpayer has filed a refund claim subject to Joint Committee Review.

body.text: Quantitative Precision Standards and the Least Advantageous Bound

Under Rev. Proc. 2011-42, the statistical validity and financial recovery of a probability sample are governed by two interconnected metrics: confidence and precision. Confidence represents the probability that the estimate generated by the sample will fall within a close range of the true total population value (the actual QREs of the entire population if examined at 100%) if the sampling and estimation procedure were repeated many times. Precision, specifically relative precision, indicates the tightness of the statistical estimate (the sampling error or achieved precision) relative to that point estimate.

In classical probability theory and under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.02(2)(c) and Section 4.03(2), a 90% two-sided confidence interval places 5% of the probability distribution in the lower tail and 5% in the upper tail; consequently, the lower bound of a 90% two-sided confidence interval is mathematically identical to the 95% one-sided lower confidence limit. Under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.03(2), the precision (achieved sampling error) is calculated by multiplying the standard error of the estimate by either: (i) the 95% one-sided confidence coefficient based on Student's t-distribution, or (ii) the normal distribution percentile value of 1.645, assuming the sample size is at least 100 in each non-100% examined stratum.

When evaluating a sample under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.02(2)(c), the IRS manages statistical uncertainty through the regulatory mechanism of the Least Advantageous 95% One-Sided Confidence Limit—commonly referred to as the Least Advantageous Bound (LAB)—which is the upper or lower 95% one-sided limit that results in the least benefit to the taxpayer. When the statistical accuracy of a sample is high—specifically, when the relative precision of the point estimate at the 95% one-sided confidence level is 10% or less—the IRS accepts the unadjusted point estimate as the extrapolated population QRE figure without penalty. However, if the statistical accuracy of the sample is low because the relative precision of the point estimate exceeds 10%, the IRS mandates a downward adjustment to the final credit calculation. When relative precision falls strictly between 10% and 15%, Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.02(2)(c) computes the allowable estimate as a linear sliding-scale interpolation between the standard point estimate and the Least Advantageous 95% One-Sided Confidence Limit; if relative precision reaches or exceeds 15%, the taxpayer must use the full Least Advantageous 95% One-Sided Confidence Limit.

Expressing this regulatory mechanism formally, let Ŷ represent the extrapolated point estimate of population QREs, SE(Ŷ) represent the standard error of the estimate, and z0.95 represent the one-sided z-distribution critical value at the 95% confidence level (or the corresponding Student's t-distribution confidence coefficient UR). The half-width of the confidence bound (achieved precision) is:
Half-width = z0.95 × SE(Ŷ)
and the relative precision (u) is defined as:
u = [z0.95 × SE(Ŷ)] / Ŷ
For a taxpayer-prepared QRE claim, the Least Advantageous 95% One-Sided Confidence Limit is the lower confidence bound (ŶL), defined as:
ŶL = Ŷ − z0.95 × SE(Ŷ)

When a taxpayer's sample yields u > 10%, the IRS applies the confidence bound that is least advantageous to the taxpayer, reducing the allowable extrapolated QRE figure toward ŶL. Specifically, in the sliding-scale interpolation range where relative precision is between 10% and 15% (0.10 < u < 0.15), the exact allowable estimate under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.02(2)(c) is determined as follows:
Estimate = Point Estimate − [(Relative Precision − 0.10) / 0.05] × (Point Estimate − Least Advantageous 95% One-Sided Confidence Limit)

Because the agency enforces the bound least advantageous to the taxpayer whenever relative precision exceeds 10%, this rule creates a powerful economic incentive for taxpayers to design high-quality samples with narrow confidence intervals. If a taxpayer fails to achieve sufficient precision through rigorous stratification and an adequate sample size, the resulting statistical imprecision automatically forces a substantial reduction in the final extrapolated credit amount, even when the initial point estimate suggests a higher figure.

Furthermore, Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.02(2)(d), Section 4.03, and Appendix C restrict variable sampling plans to four permitted mathematical estimators—Mean (direct projection), Difference (paired variables), (Combined) Ratio, and (Combined) Regression—and mandate that of all qualifying final estimates, the estimator yielding the smallest overall standard error (as an absolute value) will generally be used. To use either the Ratio or Regression estimator, Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.03(3) requires the taxpayer to first demonstrate that statistical bias inherent in those methods is negligible by satisfying four strict conditions across all non-100% tested strata: a total sample size of at least 100 units across all strata; at least 30 sample units in each individual stratum; a coefficient of variation of the paired reported variable ≤15%; and a coefficient of variation of the primary audited variable of interest ≤15% (plus, for the Ratio method, all reported values must be of the same sign). For attribute sampling plans under Section 4.04 (which estimate proportions or total counts), using the unadjusted point estimate requires achieving a relative precision of ≤10% on both the point estimate (p̂) and its complement (1 − p̂), or utilizing a simple random sample size of at least 300 units excluding dummy or null units.

body.text: Population Architecture, Sampling Units, and Stratification Design
Constructing the Sampling Frame

The foundational operational step in deploying statistical sampling is the construction of a complete and accurate population listing, known as the sampling frame. This frame must encompass every item or unit within the defined scope of the R&D credit study—such as all employees whose wages are potentially qualified or all engineering projects undertaken during the relevant tax year—and must reconcile directly to the financial general ledger, payroll registers, or Form W-2 records and the tax return. Accurately defining the population and aligning all expenses within the study's scope to a specific sampling unit are critical prerequisites for ensuring that the statistical sample reliably represents the underlying pool of QREs; any projects or expenses omitted from the sampling frame cannot be claimed later through extrapolation.

Under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Appendix A (Sampling Plan Standards) and Appendix B (Sampling Documentation Standards), taxpayers must establish a written sampling plan prior to execution and retain comprehensive execution documentation. Appendix A mandates ten written plan elements: (1) the objective of the plan, including the value being estimated and applicable tax years; (2) the population definition and reconciliation to the tax return; (3) the definition of the sampling frame; (4) the definition of the sampling unit; (5) the source of random numbers, starting point or seed, and selection method; (6) the sample size and supporting factors; (7) the method used to associate random numbers to the frame; (8) the steps ensuring that serialization of the frame is carried out independently of drawing random numbers; (9) the steps to be taken in evaluating the sampling unit; and (10) the statistical appraisal method(s) to be used. Appendix B further mandates retaining seven categories of execution records: the seed or starting point of the random numbers; the retraceable pairing of random numbers to the frame; the list of selected sampling units and evaluation results; supporting documentation such as notes, invoices, purchase orders, and project descriptions; the calculation of projected estimates to the population including standard error computations; a statement of any slips or blemishes in execution and decision rules; and the computation of all associated adjustments.
The Sampling Unit Dilemma and the Statutory Nexus Challenge

While taxpayers have operational flexibility to define the sampling unit as a business component, project, employee, cost center, department, supervisor, or contractor agreement, the selection of the sampling unit creates a major structural trade-off between data collection convenience and statutory compliance. IRS guidance strongly encourages selecting the business component—or a project that directly aligns with a business component—as the primary sampling unit because that structure maps directly to the statutory mandate under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) requiring the four-part test to be applied separately at the business component level.

In practice, however, many enterprises lack granular, project-level time-tracking software and instead account for R&D labor by cost center or department, prompting them to select non-business-component units such as individual employees or departments. For taxpayers relying on cost center or departmental accounting, the IRS LB&I Field Directive on the Use of Sampling Methodologies in Research Credit Cases explicitly suggests selecting the individual employee (via Form W-2 records) as the sampling unit rather than the project, as auditing all projects worked on by a random sample of employees is substantially more efficient than reconstructing project-wide labor across unallocated cost centers.

Selecting an employee or departmental unit, however, introduces the "nexus" challenge: the taxpayer must establish a defensible, verifiable link between the sampled expenditure (such as an employee's sampled Form W-2 wages) and the specific qualified activities performed on an underlying business component that satisfies the four-part test. Moreover, if a top-level sampled project or business component fails the four-part test as a whole (for example, failing the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold), the taxpayer must have sufficient subcomponent documentation to apply the regulatory "shrinking-back" rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to the next most significant subset of elements of the product or system. To manage operational complexity and maintain statistical validity while accommodating cost center accounting records, taxpayers may deploy a two-stage sampling methodology, first selecting a random probability sample of cost centers or departments, and subsequently drawing a second-stage random sample of the specific business components within those selected cost centers.
Stratification to Control Population Heterogeneity

R&D expenditure populations frequently exhibit high variability and heterogeneity, where a small proportion of flagship engineering programs or senior technical personnel accounts for a disproportionate share of claimed QREs alongside numerous smaller projects. Drawing an unstratified simple random sample from a highly heterogeneous population produces substantial variance (S2x), inflating the standard error of the estimate and risking an interpolation adjustment or a full Least Advantageous Bound penalty under Rev. Proc. 2011-42.

To improve the accuracy and precision of resulting estimates, stratification divides the overall heterogeneous population into separate, mutually exclusive, and internally homogeneous groups or "strata" prior to random selection. In R&D tax credit studies and IRS CAS audit plans, projects or employees are strategically stratified based on the dollar amount of claimed QREs—such as dividing the population into large, medium, and small expenditure strata—or by project type (e.g., commercial software vs. internal-use software). Additionally, as highlighted in the LB&I Field Directive, exceptionally high-value projects exceeding a predetermined dollar threshold (for example, projects exceeding $10,000,000 in claimed costs) are fully examined in a 100% stratum and kept out of the sample error projection. Because within-stratum variance (S2xi) is substantially smaller than unstratified population variance, stratification ensures adequate representation of high-value units, directly lowers overall sampling error, and enables the point estimate to satisfy the ≤10% relative precision threshold mandated by Rev. Proc. 2011-42. Importantly, Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.03(6) stipulates that strata where the sampling units or the process of evaluating those units differ from those in other strata must be excluded when calculating overall relative precision.
Substantiation, Pre-Extrapolation Adjustments, and Worked Case Analysis
Substantiation of Sampled Units and Pre-Extrapolation Integration of the 80% "Substantially All" Rules

Once random probability selection yields the final sample units, the taxpayer must execute a rigorous micro-audit of each sampled project or employee. This technical review requires gathering contemporaneous records, project logs, iterative files, emails, technical specifications, test results, and interview narratives to confirm that the sampled activities rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, computer science, or engineering and constitute a process of experimentation aimed at eliminating technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design. For every sampled unit, the taxpayer must document the specific business components involved, the employees who performed qualified services (direct research, direct supervision, or direct support), and the nature of the information sought to be discovered, as the IRS examiner retains the full entitlement to inspect all records substantiating the sampled subset.

A foundational rule of R&D statistical methodology governs how the two statutory 80% "substantially all" ("sub-all") rules—one governing employee wages and the other governing project process-of-experimentation costs—interact with mathematical extrapolation. Under the employee wage sub-all rule, if at least 80% of an employee's total services during the tax year are qualified research services, 100% of that employee's Box 1 Form W-2 wages qualify as QREs; similarly, under the project process-of-experimentation sub-all rule (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)), if at least 80% of a business component's research activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, the activity threshold is satisfied at the business component level. Statistical methodology requires that both 80% sub-all rules be applied directly to the individual sampled items before any mathematical extrapolation to the population occurs. For example, in an employee-unit sample, if a sampled engineer's qualified research time is substantiated at 80% or more, 100% of that employee's Box 1 Form W-2 wages are included as qualified expenditures within the sample numerator prior to computing the sample qualification ratio. Applying the adjustment inside the sample ensures that the extrapolated QREs accurately reflect the operation of the sub-all rule across the entire employee population, though statistical design complexity increases substantially when a single sample must accommodate both the employee and project sub-all rules simultaneously.

Following these pre-extrapolation tax law adjustments, the sample qualification ratio is projected across the total monetary value of the sampling frame to establish the total estimated QREs reported on IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities). Under the updated Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024 / January 2025) and its Final Instructions (Rev. December 2025 / February 2026), the IRS established explicit reporting rules for statistical sampling in Section G (Business Component Information), which is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (unless the taxpayer qualifies for the small-business exemption with ≤$1.5 million in QREs and ≤$50 million in average annual gross receipts at the controlled-group level, or claims credits under the ASC 730 Directive). Specifically, a taxpayer using statistical sampling under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 must still report by business component a minimum of 80% of total QREs or a maximum of 50 business components ("80%/Top 50") in Section G, append the word "sample" to the end of the business component name or identifier in Column 49(c) for each sampled component, report remaining non-sampled components in aggregate by entering "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c) with their aggregate expenditure amounts in Columns 50 through 56 (which flow directly into Section F), and attach the written statistical sampling plan to the tax return as a PDF named Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf.
Worked Hypothetical Case Analysis: IT Department Wage Extrapolation

A mid-sized technology corporation claims $10,000,000 in wage QREs attributed to its Information Technology (IT) department, which employs N = 400 individuals. The original return claim was based on a non-statistical historical departmental estimate asserting that 50% of IT staff work constituted qualified research, as the company lacked granular time-tracking software to link specific employee hours to individual projects or business components.

During the ensuing IRS examination, because project-level cost breakdowns are unavailable, the individual employee is selected as the sampling unit in accordance with the LB&I Field Directive. The IRS Computer Audit Specialist (CAS) collaborates with the examination manager to design a statistically valid random probability sample of n = 30 employees drawn from the IT department's 400-employee Form W-2 population frame for the tax year. The examination team then issues an IDR confined to those 30 sampled employees, requesting identification of the specific projects and business components each employee worked on alongside narrative descriptions of their technical activities sufficient to apply the four-part test.

To verify the mathematical mechanics step by step in this illustration, assume each sampled employee earns the departmental mean Box 1 Form W-2 wage of $25,000 (w̄ = ȳ), such that the total population wage frame (Ybase) and the total audited sample wage base (ysample) equal:

Upon completing the technical review of the 30 sampled employees, the examination reveals that exactly 15 of the 30 sampled employees devoted 80% or more of their working time (for instance, 85% actual time) to qualified research activities on valid business components, while the remaining 15 sampled employees either performed non-qualified routine work or lacked adequate nexus substantiation. Because the 80% "substantially all" rule must be applied directly to the sampled units before extrapolation (setting the employee qualification rate qi = 1.00 whenever actual qualified time is ≥80%), 100% of the Box 1 Form W-2 wages paid to the 15 qualified employees are included as qualified expenditures within the sample numerator (yqual):

Audit Defense vs. Judicial Reality: The Burden of Proof Divide
Administrative Preference Versus Litigation Exposure

A profound strategic divergence governs statistical sampling in R&D tax credit controversies: while the IRS actively favors probability sampling during administrative examinations to conserve audit resources, federal courts have consistently refused to allow taxpayers to rely on unilateral statistical sampling as primary proof of credit entitlement in litigation without a prior binding stipulation with the Service. Within the administrative arena, the IRS Internal Revenue Manual (IRM 42(18)), the LB&I Field Directive, Chief Counsel, and the Department of Justice support CAS-validated sampling plans because 100% examinations of thousands of projects are operationally unfeasible.

When an examination fails to reach administrative settlement and proceeds to litigation, however, courts prioritize the taxpayer's statutory burden of proof over the mathematical convenience of a sample. In Bayer Corp. v. United States, 850 F. Supp. 2d 522 (W.D. Pa. 2012), the federal district court rejected the taxpayer's effort to impose a statistical sampling plan on the Commissioner of Internal Revenue over government objection in a massive R&D tax credit refund suit. Bayer accounted for its research costs by cost center rather than by individual project and could not identify all of the underlying research projects or business components in the population for which research credits were claimed. The court reinforced that statistical sampling cannot be used as the primary mechanism to prove entitlement to research credits over government objection; while cost-center accounting is not automatically disqualifying, the taxpayer retains the fundamental legal burden to demonstrate through detailed documentation how all of its claimed research expenses qualify.

Similarly, in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 4759-22 (Order dated Sept. 19, 2023) and T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (decided Dec. 23, 2024) (referenced in pretrial commentary as Phoenix Design, Inc. v. Commissioner), a Tennessee-based mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) engineering firm engaged a consulting firm that identified 419 possible projects, narrowed the frame to a population of 238 projects, randomly sampled 24 projects, determined that 20 of the sampled projects involved qualified research under IRC § 41(d), and extrapolated those findings across all 238 projects to claim $461,741.00 in research credits. During Tax Court discovery, the IRS Commissioner demanded qualification details for all 238 projects, and the taxpayer moved for a protective order under Tax Court Rule 70(b)(1) to restrict discovery and trial to a subset of three to six sampled projects. In its pretrial Order denying the motion, the U.S. Tax Court held that absent a stipulation between the parties, limiting the scope of discovery and trial to a sample of research projects is improper because doing so would unlawfully relieve a taxpayer of its burden of proving entitlement to the research credits across the entire claimed population (a principle also reflected in Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, and Kapur v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-28). Furthermore, after the parties subsequently tried a nonbinding sample of three projects on the merits (Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113), the Tax Court held that none of the three trial projects satisfied either the Section 174 uncertainty test or the IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) 80% process-of-experimentation requirement, rejected shrinking back by design phase or individual employee under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), sustained 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662 pursuant to the parties' stipulation, and emphasized that an agreed nonbinding trial sample does not authorize statistical extrapolation of results to the remaining 235 projects.

body.text: The Strategic Imperative of Form 906 Closing Agreements

The judicial holdings in Bayer and Phoenix Design Group establish an essential operational imperative: compliance with Rev. Proc. 2011-42 provides a mathematically sound basis for reporting QREs on Form 6765 and negotiating an administrative settlement during an IRS examination, but it does not insulate a taxpayer from full-population discovery in court unless the IRS has formally agreed to be bound by the sample. Consequently, the most resilient audit defense strategy relies on securing a written closing agreement on IRS Form 906 (Closing Agreement on Final Determination Covering Specific Matters) early in the examination process that explicitly binds both the taxpayer and the Service to apply the extrapolated results derived from the agreed-upon sample. As underscored in Phoenix Design Group, taxpayers must also carefully distinguish between a nonbinding agreement to try representative test projects and a binding stipulation authorizing mathematical extrapolation across the population. Securing a bilateral Form 906 stipulation provides legal certainty and restricts the scope of any subsequent administrative appeal or judicial proceeding strictly to the statistical validity and substantive qualification of the sampled units, neutralizing the risk that a court will compel full-population substantiation.
Institutional Policy Recommendations and Taxpayer Defense Framework
Recommended IRS and Treasury Policy Reforms

From an institutional policy perspective, a primary administrative bottleneck in streamlining R&D examinations is the absence of a standardized IRS model sampling agreement, which currently forces local IRS Counsel to evaluate the legality and binding effect of every proposed statistical sampling agreement on an ad-hoc, case-by-case basis (Action 1: Develop Model Statistical Sampling Agreements). The IRS and Treasury should prioritize issuing standardized Model Statistical Sampling Agreements (MSAs) that codify acceptable Rev. Proc. 2011-42 methodology parameters, Least Advantageous Bound sliding-scale adjustment formulas, and binding extrapolation terms, thereby simplifying the execution of Form 906 Closing Agreements and accelerating audit resolution.

In tandem with standardized agreements, the IRS should formalize detailed nexus guidance for non-business-component sampling through an updated Revenue Procedure and enhanced Form 6765 Section G instructions (Action 2: Formalize Nexus Guidance for Non-Business-Component Sampling). Because the conflict between statutory business-component reporting under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) (and Section G's 80%/Top 50 business component requirement) and practical employee or departmental cost-center accounting remains a major driver of audit controversy—and existing IRS guidance leaves the exact documentation required to establish employee nexus highly abstract—new administrative guidance should define minimum contemporaneous documentation benchmarks required to connect sampled employee wages or contractor costs to the elimination of technical uncertainty within specific business components.

Furthermore, because the technical validity of every statistical sample rests on mandatory confirmation by an IRS Computer Audit Specialist (CAS), the Service should publish a comprehensive, standardized national CAS review checklist aligned with Appendix A and Appendix B of Rev. Proc. 2011-42 and the Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf attachment requirement (Action 3: Publish a Standardized National CAS Review Checklist). This checklist should specify the mandatory components of a taxpayer's statistical methodology report, including population frame definition and reconciliation, random number generator seeds, the statistical rationale behind stratification boundaries and 100% certainty strata, achieved precision metric calculations, and verifiable linkage between sampling units and underlying documentation, ensuring predictability across all IRS examination regions.
Taxpayer Best Practices for Audit-Ready Sampling Execution

For corporate taxpayers, defending an R&D probability sample begins with integrating statistical expertise early and contemporaneously into the return preparation workflow rather than engaging specialists solely in anticipation of an audit (Action 4: Integrate Statistical Expertise Contemporaneously and Execute Pilot Studies). Taxpayers should retain qualified statisticians alongside tax attorneys and engineers prior to filing to design a written sampling plan that satisfies the 90/10 confidence-precision standard (≤10% relative precision at the 95% one-sided confidence level), meets the sample size and coefficient-of-variation rules of Rev. Proc. 2011-42, and fulfills all requirements for the Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf return attachment. Conducting a pilot feasibility study on a small dataset prior to committing full resources verifies whether project and accounting records are complete enough to support a valid sample frame, while conducting internal workshops educates engineering and finance personnel on why specific sampled projects are selected for micro-audit interviews and how those interviews govern total corporate tax recovery.

Concurrently, taxpayers must strictly maintain full-population documentation under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) even when relying on a probability sample to compute QREs and report "Aggregate Business Components" on Form 6765 (Action 5: Maintain Full Population Documentation). Preserving foundational records across the entire population is non-negotiable under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 Section 4.05(6) and the Form 6765 instructions, providing the necessary legal backstop if a sampling stipulation is not reached and the claim is forced into full-population discovery and litigation under Bayer and Phoenix Design Group.

Finally, upon entering an IRS examination involving statistical sampling, taxpayers must aggressively prioritize negotiating and executing a written Form 906 Closing Agreement with the examination team and CAS early in the audit that explicitly binds both parties to the extrapolation methodology and outcome of the sampled analysis (Action 6: Proactively Secure a Bilateral Form 906 Closing Agreement). Locking in a bilateral Form 906 stipulation preserves administrative efficiency, prevents post-audit challenges to sample extrapolation, and forecloses full-population litigation exposure in the U.S. Tax Court or federal district court.
